# Jason Reza Jorjani — Prometheus and Atlas (2016)

## Bibliographic identity

Jason Reza Jorjani, *Prometheus and Atlas* (London: Arktos, 2016). Reviews disagree on the book's extent — 416 versus 468 pages — and the discrepancy must be resolved against the physical book before any page-range metadata is trusted; edition_status is accordingly *needed*. The book derives from Jorjani's Stony Brook dissertation, "Prometheus & Atlas: An Inquiry into the Spectral Essence of Technoscience" (PhD, Philosophy, Stony Brook University, 2015), written under a committee including Don Ihde, Edward S. Casey, Megan Craig, and Jeffrey Kripal; the book won the Parapsychological Association's 2016 Book Award. The only content this house currently carries at first hand is via the author's internal reading notes (`P1 - Jorjani - Prometheus and Atlas.md`), which cover ONLY the Prologue (pp. XII–XVI). Everything beyond the Prologue is an acquisition contract, not a holding.

## Source scholarship

The book's opening thesis, as the essay engages it, is that "All science is always already Technoscience": the practical, instrumental essence of science is ontologically prior to theoretical science, so that there never was a pure theoria which technology subsequently applied. The claim is Gestell-inflected — it stands in the lineage of Heidegger's argument that modern science is already enframed by the essence of technology — and Jorjani sharpens it into a slogan that governs the whole inquiry. From this priority claim the book develops its central category, the "spectral": that which cultural constitutions built on "binary oppositions and marginalising exclusions" must banish in order to constitute themselves. The spectral is what a settled binary order cannot admit without dissolving; technoscience, on Jorjani's account, is the historical force that renders the spectral undeniable again.

Prometheus and Atlas name the two "spectral images" of technoscience itself. Prometheus is the exploratory, challenging drive — the titan of forethought, theft of fire, and defiant provocation of the given; Atlas is the world-bearing and world-picturing titan — the cartographic power that holds up and maps a world, the condition of any world-picture at all. The pairing is the book's genuine architectural contribution as the essay reads it: technoscience shows itself not through one titanic figure but through the tension between a challenging-forth and a bearing/mapping. The essay's intended uses build on this in its own voice: (a) Prometheus–Atlas as a 0/1 pair spectrally revealed as +1/−1 under technoscience — the counterfeit transformation, with Prometheus's archetypal fall into Lucifer/Satan forms — a development the essay owns at Argued/Offered status, layered on Jorjani rather than found in him; and (b) the spectral-personae register as the point where Jorjani's vocabulary meets the Agentworld brief's own language of "human-masked ghosts from the future" and "parallax effects."

AN EXPLICIT STATUS NOTE governs this entire house: the author's existing reading notes (`P1 - Jorjani - Prometheus and Atlas.md`) cover ONLY the book's Prologue, pages XII–XVI. The Atlas/cartography chapters, any Gestell/enframing discussion in the body, and the developed spectral argument are NOT carried by any note. This house is therefore a book-level acquisition contract: the Prologue-derived cards below are usable under their stated limits, and every other intended use is fenced behind acquisition of the physical book. No essay movement may cite body-chapter content until the book is in hand and this house is extended.

The essay's developments layered on this house — Prometheus–Atlas as a 0/1 pair spectrally revealed as +1/−1 under technoscience, and Prometheus's archetypal fall into Lucifer/Satan forms — are the essay's own Argued/Offered moves and are tagged as such wherever they appear; Jorjani supplies the frame and the pair, not the development.

### Claim boundary

Jorjani's own political trajectory and the book's parapsychological claims are not endorsed and are not consumed; the essay takes only the technoscience/spectral analysis. Every use beyond the Prologue (pp. XII–XVI) awaits the book — the Atlas/cartography chapters, Gestell/enframing discussion, and the body of the spectral argument are currently uncited and uncitable. The Prologue cards themselves await print collation before any wording is promoted to quotation-ready.
